title: Metformin Protects Against Persistent Atrial Fibrillation in an Equine Model
projectDescription: Background: Horses are one of the few animals that spontaneously develop atrial fibrillation   (AF), making them a powerful model for studying AF mechanisms and treatment effects. Despite the initial effectiveness of treatment in both horses and humans, AF-induced atrial remodelling compromises long-term success. Observational studies have suggested that metformin reduces the risk of AF, but its effects on progressive AF-induced atrial remodelling have not yet been evaluated in a high-fidelity large animal model. Methods: Here, we employed a longitudinal horse model of tachypacing-induced self-sustained AF to characterize the electrical, molecular, and metabolic atrial changes over four months of disease, with and without metformin treatment. Electrophysiological and multi-omic approaches were combined with histology, echocardiography, biochemical and mitochondrial analyses to evaluate disease progression and treatment response.   Results: The horse model replicated critical aspects of AF-induced atrial remodelling observed in humans, including electrical and structural changes. Despite upregulation of metabolic genes and proteins in AF, no significant ultrastructural mitochondrial changes were detected. Metformin-treated horses were less susceptible to AF and sustained a less complex AF substrate in the right atrium after four months of disease. These effects were associated with increased activity of the metabolic regulator, AMP-activated kinase (AMPK) , changes in metabolic pathways and modulation of ion-channel gene expression. Metformin did not appear to alter left atrial substrate remodelling.  Conclusion: Metformin treatment conferred electrical protection in both the early and later stages of AF in a translationally relevant preclinical model. These findings support metformin as a lead molecul ar for AF-prevention, warranting further mechanistic and clinical studies.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Frozen tissue samples were homogenized in tissue buffer (5 nM EDTA, 25 mM NaF, 300 Sucrose, 30 nM and KH2PO4 inPMSF (final conc: 100µM) supplemented with one protease inhibitor tablet and one phosphatase inhibitor tablet per 10 ml buffer). Homogenization was performed using Lysing Matrix A tubes with beads in a Precellys 24 homogenizer (Bertin Technologies, Montigny-le-Bretonneux, France) at 5000 rpm for 20 seconds, repeated twice with a 20-second cooling interval. The homogenate was then centrifuged at 15,000 rpm for 5 minutes at 4°C. The resulting supernatant was collected and stored at -80°C.  Sample Preparation Total protein quantification was performed using the Bicinchoninic Acid Kit for Protein Determination (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, Missouri, USA). A total of 100 μg of protein was mixed with digestion buffer (0.5% SDC in 50 mM TEAB) and heat-treated for 5 min at 95 °C. Lysates were prepared following a modified filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) protocol. Proteins were reduced and alkylated in digestion buffer containing 1:50 (v:v) tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (0.5 M, Sigma) and 1:10 (v:v) 2-chloroacetamide (0.5 M, Sigma) for 30 min at 37 °C. Lysates were then digested overnight at 37 °C using Trypsin/LysC mix (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) at a 1:100 enzyme-to-protein ratio (µg/µg). The digested peptides were cleaned up using self-made stage-tips containing a Poly-styrene-divinylbenzene copolymer modified with sulfonic acid groups (SDB-RPS; 3M) material. The digested peptides were concentrated by vacuum centrifugation and reconstituted in 2% acetonitrile (Sigma) / 0.1% TFA (Sigma). Mass Spectrometry & Protein Identification The LC-MS/MS analysis was performed using a timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics) operated in positive ion mode with a mass range of 100-1700 m/z. The instrument was coupled to a Captivespray ion source and connected online to a Dionex Ultimate 3000RSnano chromatography system (Thermo Fisher). The peptides were introduced by 1 µl direct injections. Peptide seperation was achieved using an Aurora column with a CaptiveSpray inser (C18 1.6 uM particles, 15 cm, 75 μm inner diameter; IonOptics) maintained at 60 °C. A solvent gradient of buffer A (0.1 % formic acid) and buffer B (99.9% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid) was used over 28 min at flow rate of 600 nL/min. The mass spectrometer operated in data-independent acquisition (DIA) parallel accumulation–serial fragmentation (PASEF) mode with a cycle time of 1.1 seconds and a trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS) ramp time of 100 ms. The raw data files were processed using the DIA-NN software (version 1.8.0) for spectral library generation and peptide quantification.
dataProcessingProtocol: The report file generated by DIA-NN (v1.8.0) was used to acquire the count of unique proteins at a 1% FDR. Protein quantities were obtained from the unique gene list in DIA-NN (report.unique_genes_matrix.tsv) and processed using an adaptation of the DEP R-package (v1.28.0). In brief, data were filtered by excluding proteins with missing values across all samples within any one group. Following log2 transformation, multidimensional scaling (MDS) plots were created with data adjusted with the removeBatchEffect function from the EdgeR package to account for each horse contributing two samples (paired design). The data was variance-stabilized (vsn-normalized), and missing values classified as missing not at random (MNAR) were imputed using the impute.MinProb function from the DEP package. Unaccounted variance was addressed using Surrogate Variable Analysis (SVA) with the sva package (v3.50.0) and its leek method, which identified three surrogate variables that were included in the downstream linear model. Differential abundance analysis was performed using a linear model using the formula ~ 0 + Condition, where Condition was defined by anatomical region (LA, RA) and group (control, metformin, or sham), while accounting for each horse as a random effect (multilevel design). Pairwise comparisons of proteins identified differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) using the Benjamini-Hochberg method for false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment, with a threshold of FDR < 0.05.
